Part 2: Financial and Budget Procedure Rules

facts.value: Paper forecasts £200.900m of loans at 31 March 2026; our PWLB price book shows £190.900m across 11 loans at a weighted 3.3853% at the same date. Gap £10.000m — actual is £10m less than forecast.

source.title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026-2027, Appendix A (FIN/725) — Cabinet, 4 February 2026

facts.note: Paper para 2.4.1 (p.9 of Appendix A) verbatim: 'As at 31 March 2026, the Council will hold £200.900 million of loans, a decrease of £23.425 million on the previous year, as part of HRA self-financing.' Supplementary table 2.2.1 (p.3) carries the same £200.900m as 'Debt at 1 April' for 2026/27. Price book at 2026-03-31: 11 loans / £190.9m / 3.3853% (weighted). Close but does not tie exactly. Direction of the gap is toward less debt (they took £10m less than the strategy assumed). Not the sort of gap where we should paint a story either way — flag as reconciled but not exactly tied.

facts.value: 9 fresh PWLB maturity loans totalling £160,000,000 drawn on 28 March 2026 at a weighted 3.38%: £15m at 3.010% (<12m), £16m at 3.080% (1-2y), £85.9m at 3.540% (2-5y), £74m at 3.348% (5-10y). Live book before that date was 2 EIP loans at £30.9m and 4.13% weighted.

facts.note: Para 2.3.3 verbatim: 'For the purpose of setting the budget, it has been assumed that new treasury investments will be made at an average rate/yield of 3.29%, and that new long-term loans will be borrowed at an average rate of 4.00%.' The 4.00% assumption sits below the entire certainty curve today; the 3.29% investment yield is roughly in line with Bank Rate 3.75% less the OIS softening baked into the December Arlingclose forecast (which anticipates BoE cuts to 3.25% by mid-2026).

HRA MRP is nil (assets in HRA carry no MRP, standard treatment; HRA subsidy reform payment £205.9m carries no MRP). GF MRP £550k, so financing costs from MRP alone are small. summary.text:
Crawley is an HRA-heavy district — of the £223.316m CFR at 2025/26 estimate, £205.900m (92%) sits in the Housing Revenue Account (Supplementary table 1.2.3). Paragraph 2.4.1 states 'the Council will hold £200.900 million of loans, a decrease of £23.425 million on the previous year, as part of HRA self-financing' at 31 March 2026. Our PWLB price book at that date shows £190.900m across 11 loans at a weighted 3.3853% — £10m less than the paper's forecast, close but not an exact tie. Direction is toward less debt.

The most interesting figure in the file is what our book shows happened on 28 March 2026. The live book on 15 March was two EIP loans at £30.9m weighted 4.13%. On or immediately before 28 March, the Council drew nine fresh PWLB maturity loans totalling £160m at a weighted 3.38% — replacing most of the HRA settlement-era book that had matured through 2025/26. Rates achieved by bucket: 3.010% at <1yr, 3.080% 1-2yr, 3.540% 2-5yr, 3.348% 5-10yr. The paper's own budget assumption for new 2026/27 borrowing is 4.00% (para 2.3.3), which was reasonable at the time it was set — but on today's certainty curve (14 August, notice 314/26 PM) the equivalent tenors run 5.34% at 5yr and 5.83% at 10yr, roughly 180-250bp above what Crawley locked in on 28 March.

The Supplementary revises the 2026/27 CFR down from £243.352m to £241.595m and takes external debt forecast down from £225m to £219.5m, alongside a £1m addition for Land/Dwellings acquisition. The balance-sheet identity (CFR - external - OLTL = internal borrowing) ties for every one of the five forecast years to the pound.

The refinancing risk profile is contained: £15m matures inside 12 months (7.9% of the book, well under the 20% limit), and only £31m inside two years. Investment book has ranged £99.366m to £137.264m over the past year (para 2.1) and is forecast to draw down to £22-28m by 31 March 2027 to fund the accelerating capital programme. Commercial property carries an unrealised £4.866m loss on £45.705m cost — not a treasury topic and out of scope for first contact.

officer.body:
Hi Carey,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's premature-repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the Treasury Management Strategy 2026-2027 that went to Cabinet on 4 February, along with the Supplementary replacing parts of Appendix A. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A reconciliation first, which comes out close but not exact. Paragraph 2.4.1 of Appendix A forecasts £200.900m of loans at 31 March 2026, and Supplementary table 2.2.1 carries the same £200.900m as debt at 1 April 2026/27. Our PWLB file at that date holds 11 loans totalling £190.900m at a weighted 3.3853% — £10m less than the strategy assumed, so directionally toward slightly less debt taken than forecast. The balance-sheet identity (CFR less external borrowing less other long-term liabilities) ties to the pound against your Under/(over) borrowing line for every one of the five forecast years — 17,933 / 22,410 / 22,095 / 12,410 / 13,618 in the Supplementary. Worth naming both — the £10m gap is small enough that it does not change any story, and the identity holding cleanly is what proves the tables are internally consistent.

What the file also shows, and what is more interesting for a conversation, is what happened on 28 March 2026. Two weeks earlier the book was two EIP loans at £30.9m weighted 4.13% — the residue of the settlement-era paper that had matured through the year. On or immediately before 28 March you drew nine fresh PWLB maturity loans totalling £160m, at a weighted 3.38%. By tenor bucket the rates achieved were 3.010% at under-12-months, 3.080% at 1-2 years, 3.540% at 2-5 years and 3.348% at 5-10 years. Against the paper's own paragraph 2.3.3 budget assumption of 4.00% for new long-term borrowing, everything you took is inside the assumption. Against today's certainty curve (14 August, notice 314/26 PM) it looks better still — 5-year certainty is 5.34% and 10-year is 5.83%, roughly 180-250 basis points above what the 28 March book locked in. Those live rates and the SONIA path they run off are on the dashboard at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard.

The implication we would raise, carefully, is on the incremental need. The Supplementary revises the 2026/27 net financing need up to £23.829m and 2027/28 to £33.484m. Any drawdown against those numbers is what gets priced against the current curve, not the 4.00% assumption in the paper. We can't say what your right answer is — that turns on cash timing and the shape of the capital programme, which we don't see — but the gap is worth having as a modelled input to the mid-year update.

While we have you looking, a small pattern from the wider file. July's sector PWLB drawings across all councils were £368m from just 19 borrowers — a thin month, and the borrowers were a mix of HRA refinancings and non-treasury capital. The breakdown by tenor and by council is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity. It gives you a sense of what shape of activity is going through in the same window your 28 March draw sat in, and what the sector has been paying since. On our side, we hold PWLB only, so if you have any LOBO, bank or market debt outside PWLB none of the above touches it.

On training, four fit. HRA self-financing: refinancing the 2012 settlement stock is written for exactly the situation your book is in. Reading the PWLB certainty curve covers the mechanics of what your paper quotes at gilt+0.80. Liability Benchmark: the essentials is worth watching given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Code updates — your paper already uses it (Appendix A section 1.3.2) which is ahead of many. And Members' introduction to treasury is the one to point Cabinet and OSC members at ahead of the next strategy cycle. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

One caveat before the sources. The 28 March timing story is ours, reconstructed from file snapshots, and the indicative break costs the platform generates for the book are indicative only — the DMO's premature-repayment quote is the only binding one, and we model no MRP or accounting treatment on top.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing.
